subject: Logan et al. (2011)
object: Logan et al. (2011) used phased haplotype analysis followed by targeted exome sequencing to identify mutations in the MEGF10 gene in patients with a previously unrecognized type of infantile myopathy. They named it early-onset myopathy, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia (EMARDD).

subject: Logan et al. (2011)
object: Logan et al. (2011) described an infantile myopathy with diaphragmatic weakness, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia. They noted that infantile myopathies with diaphragmatic paralysis are genetically heterogeneous and that clinical symptoms do not help distinguish between them.

subject: Logan et al. (2011)
object: Logan et al. (2011) reported that MEGF10 is highly expressed in activated satellite cells and regulates their proliferation, differentiation, and fusion into multinucleated myofibers. These processes are greatly reduced in muscle from individuals with EMARDD.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease. Weakness began by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It was mainly axial and proximal, included facial weakness, and stabilized in adolescence. Neck contractures appeared in infancy, and elbow, knee, and heel-cord contractures developed by adulthood. Serum CK was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion, and from age 10 to 11 years all had respiratory problems requiring nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure. All 3 had hypernasal speech; 1 was born with a cleft palate and another had a midline palatal ridge.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) found that muscle biopsies from family 1030 showed dystrophic features: fatty replacement of myofibers, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. They also showed myopathic features, namely moth-eaten fibers and minicores, the minicores mainly in type I fibers. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent. Type I fibers slightly predominated and varied more in size than type II fibers.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) carried out a genomewide linkage scan in family 1030 that gave positive LOD scores at 16 loci. MEGF10 lay within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329. The analysis excluded SEPN1, RYR1, ACTA1, and TPM3.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) combined whole genome sequencing with linkage data and found that affected members of family 1030 were compound heterozygous for 2 missense mutations in MEGF10, c.976T-C (p.C326R) in exon 10 and c.2320T-C (p.C774R) in exon 19. The mutations were in trans and segregated with the disease in all 6 family members. Both were absent from dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, and the Exome Sequencing Project, and from 715 and 645 genotyped controls, respectively. Each mutation replaces a cysteine that is conserved in 43 of 43 species, in EGF-like domains 6 and 16, and the authors predicted that this disrupts disulfide bonds.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) described a sporadic female patient (105-1) of Caucasian origin with distant Portuguese ancestry who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease. She had hypotonia at several weeks of age, a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive from poor feeding, blue sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. In childhood she had frequent pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems. At age 10 years her serum CK was 302 U/L. Her scoliosis reached 20 degrees by age 12, and she had mild, nonprogressive proximal and facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, which electron microscopy confirmed.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) sequenced MEGF10 in 190 patients with unexplained myopathies and found 1 patient (105-1) with a single heterozygous mutation, c.211C-T (p.R71W), in the emilin domain. The variant was absent from public databases and from 699 controls, and it was inherited from an unaffected parent. Sequencing of muscle cDNA did not reveal a second mutation. Because the patient's clinical and histologic features resembled those of family 1030, the authors suggested she may carry a second MEGF10 mutation they could not detect.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) observed that patients with MEGF10 missense mutations had a phenotype similar to, but milder than, the severe congenital myopathy previously reported with nonsense and frameshift mutations. They attributed this to residual MEGF10 function in their patients, in contrast to total loss of expression in the earlier families. Minicores were prominent in their missense-mutation patients but had not been noted in the families with null mutations.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) knocked down megf10 in zebrafish with 4 different splice-blocking morpholinos. The morphants had curled or bent tails, impaired swimming, reduced response to touch, and unhatched eggs. They also showed reduced birefringence, disrupted somite boundaries, gaps between myofibers, and myofibrillar disorganization on electron microscopy, which the authors took as consistent with a myopathic process.

subject: Boyden et al. (2012)
object: Boyden et al. (2012) hypothesized that loss of MEGF10 function causes satellite cells to differentiate excessively, depleting the self-renewing cells that regenerate damaged muscle fibers. They suggested that satellite cell dysfunction could be a pathogenic mechanism shared with SEPN1-related multiminicore disease.

subject: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013)
object: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) noted that a family with a milder phenotype carried compound heterozygous missense mutations C326R and C774R in MEGF10. The 3 affected individuals were in their third decade, one was still ambulatory, and they needed only noninvasive nocturnal ventilatory support. C774R paired with a nonsense mutation had been seen in a severely affected family. The authors suggested that C774R is as deleterious as a nonsense mutation, while C326R may be less consequential.

subject: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013)
object: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) found that MEGF10 C326R and C774R mutants overexpressed in HEK293T and C2C12 cells showed reduced tyrosine phosphorylation. The reduction was severe for C774R and mild for C326R. Neither mutation changed subcellular localization. C774R showed reduced N-glycosylation and weaker c-Src binding and phosphorylation. The authors noted that these patterns are consistent with the genotype-phenotype correlation in the human disease.

subject: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013)
object: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) identified Y1030 as the major tyrosine phosphorylation site of MEGF10 and showed that it is phosphorylated at least in part by c-Src, which co-immunoprecipitated with MEGF10. Overexpressing wild-type MEGF10 or the phosphomimetic Y1030D mutant increased C2C12 myoblast proliferation, but the Y1030F mutant did not.

subject: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013)
object: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) suggested that MEGF10 myopathy may be caused by a defect in muscle satellite cell proliferation resulting from impaired MEGF10 tyrosine phosphorylation signaling. They also suggested that the 16th EGF-like domain may matter more for signaling than the 6th.

subject: Liewluck et al. (2016)
object: Liewluck et al. (2016) reported 2 sisters who had respiratory insufficiency beginning in adulthood, followed later by limb weakness. Both sisters had scoliosis, hyperlaxity of the distal joints, and high-arched feet. A right triceps muscle biopsy from one sister showed multiple minicores, and her EMG showed myopathic changes with fibrillation potentials and myotonic discharges.

subject: Liewluck et al. (2016)
object: In 2 sisters with adult-onset myopathy with minicores, respiratory insufficiency, and scoliosis, Liewluck et al. (2016) used next-generation sequencing to identify compound heterozygous missense variants in the MEGF10 gene: c.230G>A (p.Arg77Gln) and c.1833T>G (p.Cys611Trp). The authors concluded that MEGF10 mutations can cause myopathy with respiratory insufficiency beginning in adulthood.

subject: Takayama et al. (2016)
object: Takayama et al. (2016) reported a Japanese patient with the milder phenotype of MEGF10 myopathy who carried compound heterozygous MEGF10 mutations: a splice site mutation (c.2981-2A>G) and a novel missense mutation (p.Cys810Tyr).

subject: Takayama et al. (2016)
object: Takayama et al. (2016) noted that cysteine mutations in the extracellular EGF-like domain of MEGF10 may be responsible for the milder phenotype. They reported 2 Japanese patients: one with the severe EMARDD phenotype who had a novel homozygous frameshift mutation (c.131_132del), and one with the milder phenotype who had a compound heterozygous mutation that included the cysteine missense mutation p.Cys810Tyr. The authors concluded that these findings indicated a genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.

subject: Takayama et al. (2016)
object: Takayama et al. (2016) stated that mutations in MEGF10 cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD) as well as a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy. At the time of their report, 6 families with EMARDD and 1 with the milder disorder had been described.

subject: Saha et al. (2017)
object: Saha et al. (2017) found that shRNA-mediated knockdown of Megf10, as well as overexpression of the pathogenic human MEGF10 p.C774R mutation, impaired proliferation and migration of C2C12 myoblasts.

subject: Saha et al. (2017)
object: Saha et al. (2017) showed by reciprocal coimmunoprecipitation that Megf10 and Notch1 interact via their respective intracellular domains, and that these interactions were impaired by the pathogenic p.C774R mutation. They suggested that Megf10 regulation of myoblast function is mediated at least in part via interactions with Notch signaling components, and that defects in these interactions may contribute to the pathogenesis of EMARDD.

subject: Saha et al. (2017)
object: Saha et al. (2017) found that myoblasts from Megf10-null mice and Megf10/mdx double-knockout mice showed impaired proliferation and migration compared with myoblasts from wildtype and mdx mice, and that the double-knockout mice showed histologic abnormalities not observed in either single mutant mouse.

subject: Harris et al. (2018)
object: Harris et al. (2018) reported a 66-year-old man with a 20-year history of progressive proximal and distal weakness of the upper and lower limbs, facial weakness, and dysphagia. In his 50s, while still ambulant, he developed respiratory failure that required ventilation. Muscle biopsy showed myopathic changes with aggregation of myofibrillar proteins.

subject: Harris et al. (2018)
object: In a 66-year-old man with adult-onset MEGF10-related myopathy, Harris et al. (2018) used exome sequencing to identify a novel essential splice-site variant in the MEGF10 gene (c.1426+1G>T). The variant was described in the context of recessive MEGF10 mutations.

subject: Harris et al. (2018)
object: In the same patient, Harris et al. (2018) identified by exome sequencing a novel missense variant in the MEGF10 gene, c.352T>C (p.Cys118Arg), which was the second mutation found alongside the c.1426+1G>T splice-site variant.

subject: Harris et al. (2018)
object: Harris et al. (2018) reviewed all 20 reported cases with MEGF10 mutations and confirmed a genotype-phenotype correlation. In patients with at least 1 null mutation, respiratory dysfunction began in the first year of life. In patients with 2 missense mutations, respiratory dysfunction began at about 10 years of age or much later. The authors stated that their findings expanded the phenotype to include onset in the fifth decade.

subject: Saha et al. (2019)
object: Saha et al. (2019) ran a small-molecule screen in Megf10-deficient myoblasts and identified 2 selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), sertraline and escitalopram. Follow-up testing in Megf10 -/- mouse myoblasts, induced pluripotent stem cell-derived myoblasts from patients with MEGF10 myopathy, Drosophila deficient in the MEGF10 homolog Drpr, and megf10 mutant zebrafish showed that sertraline was highly effective at relieving abnormalities in all of these models and restored Notch1 deficiencies. The authors concluded that SSRIs, especially sertraline, show promise as therapies for MEGF10 myopathy and suggested that the mechanism may involve the Notch pathway.

subject: Li et al. (2021)
object: Li et al. (2021) cultured single myofibers isolated from the extensor digitorum longus muscles of Megf10-null mice and wildtype mice. At 24, 48, and 72 hours, fewer satellite cells had detached from Megf10-null myofibers than from wildtype myofibers. The authors concluded that Megf10 deficiency is associated with impaired satellite cell activation and migration.

subject: Li et al. (2021)
object: Li et al. (2021) found fewer Pax7+/MyoD+ activated satellite cells associated with Megf10-null myofibers than with wildtype myofibers, and these cells migrated shorter distances. Satellite cells detached from Megf10-null myofibers also had fewer MyoD-positive nuclei. The authors concluded that Megf10 contributes to an early stage of satellite cell activation, during which the cells migrate to target myofibers.

subject: Li et al. (2021)
object: Li et al. (2021) injured the tibialis anterior muscle of Megf10-null and wildtype mice with 3 sequential intramuscular barium chloride injections, starting at 2 months of age, to deplete the satellite cell pool. Compared with wildtype muscle, injured Megf10-null muscle showed significantly reduced regeneration, with pockets of atrophic fibers, clusters of small myofibers with internalized nuclei, and greater variability in fiber size. Fibronectin staining showed more fibrosis in injured Megf10-null muscle.

subject: Li et al. (2021)
object: Li et al. (2021) suggested that impaired satellite cell function and impaired muscle regeneration caused by MEGF10 deficiency could help explain why the clinical manifestations of MEGF10 myopathy persist. They noted that muscle function generally does not improve in affected patients.

subject: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021)
object: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) reported a boy (patient 2) from a consanguineous Saudi family (parents were first cousins) with a mild form of MEGF10-related congenital myopathy. He had generalized hypotonia from the newborn period, after a pregnancy with decreased fetal movements. He had feeding difficulties, choking, recurrent aspiration pneumonia and motor delay, but he sat at 21 months and was walking independently, though running slowly, at age 9 years. He had no major cognitive deficits and did not need long-term oxygen. On examination he had plagiocephaly, facial diplegia, a high-arched palate, low-set ears, mild thoracic scoliosis with spinal rigidity, axial-predominant hypotonia, proximal weakness, a positive Gowers sign, areflexia and joint hyperlaxity. Creatine kinase was normal, nerve conduction was normal, EMG showed neurogenic changes, and a modified barium study showed mild oral dysphagia. A sister with a similar phenotype died at 18 months of respiratory infections.

subject: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021)
object: In patient 2, AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) used a muscular dystrophy and myopathy gene panel and found a homozygous splice-site variant in the MEGF10 gene (c.2980+5G>C, NM_032446.2). Sanger sequencing confirmed it. RT-PCR on RNA from the patient's lymphoblastoid cells showed a larger, aberrant transcript, and sequencing showed that it retained 85 bp of intron 23. The panel also found a heterozygous PRKAG3 variant (c.364dupA, p.Thr122Asnfs*11).

subject: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021)
object: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) also reported a severely affected boy (patient 1) from an unrelated consanguineous Saudi family. He had congenital hypotonia after a pregnancy with decreased fetal movements, and neonatal seizures that responded to phenobarbital. He had facial diplegia, ptosis, camptodactyly, pectus excavatum, scoliosis with butterfly vertebrae, right diaphragmatic eventration, developmental dysplasia of the hip, nephrolithiasis and absent tendon reflexes. He was never able to sit, needed gastrostomy feeding and supplemental oxygen, and had myopathic EMG changes. His muscle biopsy was essentially normal. He died at 8 months of respiratory failure, and an affected sister died at 11 months.

subject: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021)
object: In patient 1, who had the severe phenotype, AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) used a myopathy gene panel and found a homozygous frameshift variant in the MEGF10 gene (c.3132dupA, p.Glu1045Argfs*22, NM_032446.2).

subject: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021)
object: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) noted that the 2 different MEGF10 variants were associated with different severity. The homozygous frameshift variant caused a severe phenotype with death in infancy. The homozygous splice-site variant caused a milder, ambulant phenotype resembling an axial-predominant myopathy with scoliosis and spinal rigidity.

subject: Fujii et al. (2022)
object: Fujii et al. (2022) reported a man with progressive weakness that began in his thirties, who developed severe respiratory failure at age 66 years. His muscle biopsy showed no clear cores.

subject: Fujii et al. (2022)
object: In a man with adult-onset progressive myopathy and respiratory failure, Fujii et al. (2022) identified a novel mutation, p.G739R, in the MEGF10 gene.

subject: Fujii et al. (2022)
object: Fujii et al. (2022) summarized their patient and previously reported patients with MEGF10 mutations and found that patients with missense mutations in at least 1 allele had significantly later onset than those with biallelic truncating mutations. They noted that some reported patients with the mild variant phenotype had no clear cores.

subject: Croci et al. (2022)
object: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man, born to healthy consanguineous parents, who had a congenital myopathic phenotype with weak suction, elbow contractures and scoliosis from the first months of life. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation and needed resuscitation for asphyxia. Motor development and intellect were normal. He then developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia and respiratory involvement, and needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy, cleft palate, global areflexia, contractures of the elbows and ankles, and hyperlordosis. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, and cardiac studies were normal.

subject: Croci et al. (2022)
object: Croci et al. (2022) found that the patient's first muscle biopsy, taken at age 5 years, showed nonspecific changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions and minicores. Electrophysiologic studies were normal apart from reduced amplitude of the muscle evoked potential. The authors proposed that the minicores seen in the late-onset group may result from longstanding myofibrillar pathology that begins in infancy.

subject: Croci et al. (2022)
object: In an Italian man with a progressive form of mvEMARDD, Croci et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous missense variant in the MEGF10 gene, c.2096G-C (p.Cys699Ser; NM_001256545.2). Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant, and both consanguineous parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was absent from ClinVar and gnomAD, changes a conserved cysteine in an EGF-like domain, and was predicted to be damaging by in silico tools. It was classified as likely pathogenic.

subject: Croci et al. (2022)
object: Croci et al. (2022) noted that missense variants in MEGF10 have been associated with later onset and a milder course. Their patient carried a missense variant but had early-onset myopathy with a progressive course. The authors proposed that MEGF10-related phenotypes form a continuum rather than a dichotomy between classic EMARDD and mvEMARDD.
